transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Runtime LTS technical deep dive (backports, upgrade/rollback, audit evidence)
Date: 2025-11-26
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 min

Attendees
- Connor O'Brien (Redwood Inference)
- Noah Patel (Redwood Inference)
- Sahana Iyer (Redwood Inference)
- Vivek Kulkarni (Redwood Inference)
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood Inference)
- Priya Nair (HelioBank)
- Dan Whitaker (HelioBank)
- Miguel Santos (HelioBank)
- Jenna Lee (HelioBank)

Summary (auto-generated)
- HelioBank requested details on Redwood’s planned Runtime LTS channel, including branching model, backport policy, and upgrade/rollback process for Private deployments.
- Redwood walked through proposed LTS guarantees: slower-change cadence, defined support window, patch release process with SRE regression gates, and enterprise-focused release notes.
- HelioBank emphasized audit evidence requirements (traceability from ticket → PR → artifact), signing/provenance, and predictable maintenance windows.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Why LTS vs regular release train
- LTS branch naming/cut criteria and support duration
- Backport eligibility tiers and approval workflow
- Perf regression gates and canary/rollback
- Private/VPC upgrade + version pinning
- Audit evidence, attestations, and release artifacts

Questions (auto-generated)
- What changes are allowed into LTS (bugfix vs perf vs refactor)?
- How do you handle emergency security fixes vs monthly patches?
- How do we pin, roll forward, and roll back in Private without surprises?
- What artifacts and logs can you provide for audit?

Transcript

[00:00] Connor O'Brien: Alright, cool. Folks are joining. Um, thanks everyone. This is Connor from Redwood. I run release engineering on the runtime side. The goal today is, like, go deeper than the deck—talk through what “LTS” means for us, how backports work, and specifically your upgrade and rollback requirements for Private.

[00:18] Priya Nair: Perfect. Yeah, thanks Connor. We’ve been burned on “stable” branches before. So we want the details and what you’ll actually commit to.

[00:25] Connor O'Brien: Yep. Totally fair. Quick intros? I have Noah, Sahana, Vivek, Naomi on as well.

[00:32] Noah Patel: Hey, Noah. I’m the runtime LTS architect on our side, owning branching model and backport policy.

[00:37] Sahana Iyer: Sahana. I do CI/build automation, release gates.

[00:41] Vivek Kulkarni: Vivek, product lead for Private deployments.

[00:44] Naomi Feldman: Naomi, compliance requirements and enterprise readiness.

[00:48] Dan Whitaker: Dan, SRE lead here. I care about regressions and rollback.

[00:51] Miguel Santos: Miguel, security and GRC.

[00:53] Jenna Lee: Jenna, ML engineering, I’m usually the one filing “hey the throughput dropped” tickets.

[00:58] Connor O'Brien: Great. Priya, you want to set context on what’s driving this?

[01:02] Priya Nair: Sure. We’re running your runtime in a VPC deployment. We can’t take “every two weeks there’s a new minor” style upgrades. We have a CAB, we have maintenance windows, and we have audit requirements. But we also can’t sit on something forever if there’s security fixes. So we want a stable line we can pin to, and a predictable patch cadence. And release notes that are not like… 400 lines of internal refactors.

[01:29] Connor O'Brien: Yeah. That matches what we’re hearing. So the big idea: we’ll keep the normal release train moving fast—new kernels, new scheduling features, model onboarding, etc. LTS is a separate channel for Dedicated/Private/enterprise where changes are tightly scoped.

[01:44] Noah Patel: Maybe I’ll lay down definitions. When we say Runtime LTS, we mean the serving runtime layer: kernel + scheduling + the pieces that impact latency/throughput, stability, correctness. Not like, every UI thing.

[01:58] Jenna Lee: And does that include model configs? Like quant profiles?

[02:02] Noah Patel: Good question. We’re treating “runtime engine” plus “supported model adapters” as part of the LTS compatibility surface, but we’re not going to be adding new model families into an existing LTS branch. So you’ll get bug/security fixes for what’s already supported in that branch cut.

[02:20] Priya Nair: Okay, so it’s not like you cut LTS and then later you shove in a whole new attention backend.

[02:24] Noah Patel: Exactly. That would violate the point.

[02:28] Connor O'Brien: The branch model we’re proposing is like runtime-1.20-lts, as an example, cut from a known-good minor release. Then patch tags on top, like 1.20-lts.1, .2, etc.

[02:42] Dan Whitaker: What’s “known-good”? Like, based on production canary or just unit tests?

[02:48] Sahana Iyer: It’s both. The cut criteria we’re drafting: must have passed the full CI matrix, GPU determinism checks, and then a canary in at least one Redwood region with real traffic patterns. Plus a perf baseline run.

[03:03] Dan Whitaker: Determinism checks meaning… bit-for-bit?

[03:07] Sahana Iyer: Not fully bit-for-bit on all GPUs, but reproducible build outputs and consistent perf/functional metrics within bounds. Also artifact signing and provenance.

[03:18] Miguel Santos: That’s the part I care about. When you say “provenance,” do you mean SLSA-style attestation? Or is it like, “we promise we built it”?

[03:26] Naomi Feldman: We’re working toward attestations you can store as evidence: build pipeline identity, source commit, dependency versions, and artifact hashes. Some customers call it SLSA-ish. The commitment language matters, but directionally yes.

[03:41] Miguel Santos: And SBOM?

[03:42] Naomi Feldman: For the runtime image, yes, we can provide an SBOM artifact or at minimum a dependency manifest. We have to confirm format your auditors prefer.

[03:52] Priya Nair: Okay. Let’s talk support window. What are you thinking? 6 months? 12? 24?

[03:59] Connor O'Brien: The current proposal is 12 months of support for an LTS line, with an overlap window so you can plan migrations. Like, we wouldn’t end support the day the next LTS appears.

[04:11] Dan Whitaker: Twelve is fine if the overlap is real. We need time to validate.

[04:15] Jenna Lee: Patch cadence? We can’t take weekly patches.

[04:19] Connor O'Brien: Monthly regular patch cadence is what we’re aiming for. Plus “out-of-band” for critical security or a severe correctness issue.

[04:29] Priya Nair: How do you define “critical”? Because everything is critical when it breaks.

[04:34] Noah Patel: That’s where the backport policy tiers come in. We’re defining eligibility tiers.

[04:39] Noah Patel: Tier 0 is security fixes (CVE-class, or high severity). Tier 1 is correctness/data integrity issues, crashes, deadlocks. Tier 2 is performance regressions relative to the LTS baseline. Tier 3 is “nice to have” improvements—generally not eligible.

[04:56] Jenna Lee: Performance regression: like, if my p95 goes up 10%?

[05:01] Noah Patel: Yes, though we’ll quantify it. The SRE gate doc we’re aligning with is thresholds on p95 and p99 latency and throughput on the standard bench set.

[05:11] Dan Whitaker: Wait, is the bench set public? Because our workload is not your benchmark.

[05:16] Connor O'Brien: The baseline suite is our standard “perf canary” set. We can also incorporate a customer-specific eval for your staging if you want, but we can’t block LTS on every customer’s workload obviously.

[05:28] Dan Whitaker: Sure. But at least don’t regress the general case.

[05:31] Sahana Iyer: That’s the goal. For LTS patches, we require: (1) unit/integration, (2) GPU functional, (3) perf suite baseline with thresholds, and (4) canary duration.

[05:43] Priya Nair: Canary duration—how long are you thinking?

[05:45] Sahana Iyer: We’ve been debating 24 hours versus 72. For patch releases it’s likely 24 hours minimum in a controlled environment, and longer if the change is riskier.

[05:56] Dan Whitaker: Riskier according to what? Like, if you touch scheduler.

[06:00] Noah Patel: Exactly. We’ll label backports by risk. Changes in the scheduler, KV cache behavior, memory management—those are high risk. Pure logging changes are low risk.

[06:11] Connor O'Brien: And the release notes will reflect that. The whole “enterprise release notes” thing is: what changed, why you should care, risk level, any behavior change, mitigation, rollback notes.

[06:25] Jenna Lee: That is what we want. The current notes are like “refactor X” “rename Y”. It doesn’t help.

[06:31] Connor O'Brien: Yeah. For LTS we’ll filter out internal refactors unless they change behavior.

[06:38] Miguel Santos: I want to understand the approval controls. Who signs off? Is it two reviewers? Is there an audit trail?

[06:44] Noah Patel: The policy we’re drafting: any LTS backport PR needs (a) original PR link, (b) justification of eligibility tier, (c) test evidence attached, and (d) approvals. Approval matrix: runtime code owners plus release engineering sign-off, and for security fixes, security reviewer.

[07:03] Miguel Santos: Is that tracked in GitHub or some internal tool?

[07:07] Connor O'Brien: GitHub labels + PR template, plus linkage to a ticket. Internally we track it, but the artifact is in GitHub so you can export evidence. We’re also building a “backport helper” tool to standardize commit messages and include provenance references.

[07:23] Priya Nair: For us, audit wants traceability: issue number, approver, test run IDs, artifact hash.

[07:30] Sahana Iyer: We can provide build run IDs and attestations. Artifact hash definitely. The “test run IDs” is basically CI run links. We can also produce a release evidence bundle per patch.

[07:43] Naomi Feldman: To set expectation: for some regulated environments, we provide a release packet: list of changes, approvals, CI results references, hashes, and signing keys used. That’s where we’re headed for LTS.

[07:55] Miguel Santos: Key management: do you use your own signing key? Can we verify? Is it rotated? Where is it stored? HSM?

[08:02] Naomi Feldman: We use managed key infrastructure with restricted access. For contract specifics we’ll pull in our security reviewer (Marcus) if needed. Verification: you’ll have public verification material to validate signatures.

[08:16] Dan Whitaker: Switching to upgrade/rollback. Our biggest fear is we upgrade and then realize our custom routing rules break because of some config schema change.

[08:25] Vivek Kulkarni: Totally. So for Private, we’re aligning LTS with stricter compatibility guarantees. The installer/Helm charts will allow pinning to LTS tags. Supported upgrade paths will be “within an LTS line” forward (e.g., 1.20-lts.2 to .3), and then “LTS to next LTS” with an explicit playbook.

[08:44] Priya Nair: Can we skip patches? Like go from .1 to .4?

[08:48] Vivek Kulkarni: Yes, generally, within a line. But we’ll call out if a patch includes a migration step that wants you to go sequentially. Our goal is to avoid migrations in LTS patches unless it’s required for a security fix.

[09:04] Jenna Lee: Is there any database migration? We mostly run stateless for runtime, but we have some metadata.

[09:10] Vivek Kulkarni: Runtime itself is mostly stateless. Where you can see “migration-like” behavior is config schema or metrics naming changes. Those will be treated as high risk and usually avoided.

[09:22] Dan Whitaker: Rollback: can we roll back the runtime container tag and be done? Or are there side effects like cache format changes?

[09:29] Noah Patel: Great question. Cache format changes are exactly the kind of thing we won’t do in LTS unless we absolutely have to. If we must, the release notes will include “rollback notes,” and we’ll include mitigation like “drain pods and clear cache.”

[09:45] Dan Whitaker: Okay, but make it explicit. We’ve had vendors say “rollback is supported” and then you roll back and the system thrashes.

[09:52] Connor O'Brien: Agreed. For LTS, we’re making rollback validation part of the release checklist. Like, we actually test “upgrade then rollback” in a staging environment.

[10:02] Sahana Iyer: At least for the reference deployment. If you have a custom layer, you’d still need to validate, but we’ll provide guidance.

[10:12] Priya Nair: And how does notification work? We need advance notice. Even security patches have process.

[10:18] Connor O'Brien: For regular monthly patches: we can give you a calendar, and release notes draft ahead of time, within reason. For security out-of-band: we’ll follow an embargo process, limited early notice if needed, then release when safe.

[10:33] Miguel Santos: Embargo process is key. We can’t have it in a public repo before we patch.

[10:38] Naomi Feldman: Correct. For embargoed fixes we use restricted comms and limited visibility until disclosure. The backport process will reflect that.

[10:49] Jenna Lee: Can we talk about what qualifies for backport? Because you said perf regression fixes are eligible. But what if there’s a perf improvement we want—like 20% throughput from a kernel change.

[10:59] Noah Patel: That’s where we draw a line. Pure “improvement” is usually not LTS. But if you have a regression relative to the LTS baseline—like you upgrade within the LTS line and perf drops—that is eligible to fix. Also, if a known issue at branch cut is severe and we have a very surgical fix, maybe, but that would be exceptional.

[11:20] Priya Nair: That’s fine. We’re not asking you to add features. We’re asking you to stop surprising us.

[11:26] Connor O'Brien: Exactly. The “normal” channel is where the improvements land.

[11:31] Dan Whitaker: I want to know about the “minimal diff” idea. In the past, vendors say they backport but actually they bring in a chain of dependencies.

[11:39] Noah Patel: Yep. Our backport policy requires minimal-diff. If a fix depends on refactors, we either (a) re-implement the fix in a smaller form for the LTS branch, or (b) we decide it’s too risky and we don’t backport.

[11:54] Jenna Lee: Will you ever say “no”? Like customer asks.

[11:56] Connor O'Brien: Yes. And we’ll document why. Because LTS promise only works if we decline risky changes.

[12:03] Priya Nair: Can we get SLAs around that? Like response time to backport requests.

[12:09] Connor O'Brien: We can define intake and triage SLAs. For enterprise, typically we commit to acknowledging within X business days, and then target patch inclusion based on severity.

[12:21] Miguel Santos: On audit, one more: do you maintain a “known issues” list? Auditors ask, “what are known limitations and compensating controls.”

[12:29] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we’re maintaining an LTS known-issues and exclusions list. It’s important for transparency. For example, certain model families might be excluded from LTS support, or known perf cliffs at extreme sequence lengths.

[12:44] Jenna Lee: Sequence length cliffs… yes. We saw something around 16k.

[12:47] Noah Patel: Right. Those are the sorts of things that will be called out.

[12:52] Dan Whitaker: Can you talk about “exclusions” a bit? Like what’s explicitly out of LTS.

[12:57] Noah Patel: Big refactors, new kernel backends, scheduler policy changes that alter fairness characteristics, and major dependency bumps. Also “experimental” flags.

[13:09] Priya Nair: Dependency bumps is a big one. We don’t want CUDA or driver assumptions to change mid-line.

[13:14] Sahana Iyer: Exactly. For LTS we’ll pin a supported GPU/driver matrix. If there’s a security fix requiring a base image bump, we’ll treat it as high risk and do more extensive validation.

[13:28] Dan Whitaker: That should be in release notes too.

[13:30] Connor O'Brien: Yup.

[13:33] (crosstalk)

[13:34] Jenna Lee: Can you clarify “artifact locations”? For Private, we pull from your registry. We need to know the naming and tags.

[13:42] Vivek Kulkarni: LTS artifacts will be under a distinct tag scheme. For example, runtime:1.20-lts.3. The installer and Helm charts will accept that tag and validate it. We’re also adding guardrails like “don’t accidentally pull latest.”

[13:58] Priya Nair: We had that happen with another vendor, “latest” got pulled.

[14:01] Vivek Kulkarni: Yeah, we’ll make LTS opt-in and explicit.

[14:06] Miguel Santos: Are artifacts immutable? Tag immutability is a requirement.

[14:10] Connor O'Brien: For LTS, yes. Once published, the tag is immutable, and we publish hashes. If there’s an issue, we publish a new patch tag, we don’t overwrite.

[14:21] Miguel Santos: Good.

[14:23] Dan Whitaker: So, about rollback triggers. How do you decide to yank a patch?

[14:29] Sahana Iyer: We don’t “yank” in the sense of rewriting. But we can issue an advisory: “don’t deploy 1.20-lts.4, use .5.” Rollback triggers are based on error rate, latency regression beyond thresholds, or critical incident in canary.

[14:45] Dan Whitaker: Do you have an error budget concept for release?

[14:48] Sahana Iyer: Yes. LTS patches have stricter gating and the canary must not blow the SLOs. The SRE team owns those gates.

[14:58] Priya Nair: Is this canary in your hosted environment, or for Private too?

[15:03] Connor O'Brien: We can canary internally and on our Dedicated fleets. For Private, we can provide a recommended canary procedure: upgrade a subset of nodes, monitor, then roll out.

[15:15] Dan Whitaker: We’ll do that. But we need to know what to monitor.

[15:19] Vivek Kulkarni: We’ll include recommended dashboards and alerts. Also Helm values to enable recommended monitoring for LTS by default.

[15:29] Jenna Lee: Can we bring up the “upgrade pain point” we had? We upgraded runtime minor and saw token latency spike but only for streaming responses.

[15:38] Noah Patel: Yeah, that’s exactly the kind of regression that should not happen in LTS. And if it did, it would be Tier 2 and would get fixed as a patch.

[15:49] Priya Nair: The other pain: behavior changes. Like tool calling formatting changed and we had to adjust.

[15:54] Noah Patel: LTS will treat outward behavior changes as almost always not allowed. If unavoidable, we document it as “behavior change” with migration instructions and risk level. But we aim to avoid.

[16:08] Miguel Santos: And do you have deprecation policy? Like if something is going away.

[16:12] Connor O'Brien: For LTS, deprecations are effectively frozen. If something is deprecated in mainline, it won’t be removed in an existing LTS line.

[16:21] Priya Nair: That’s important.

[16:24] Connor O'Brien: Can I ask a couple qualifiers? Timeline pressure? Are you trying to close procurement on this?

[16:30] Priya Nair: We’re evaluating now. We have a decision by end of Q1. But our legal team is already asking about support windows and patch processes.

[16:41] Connor O'Brien: Got it.

[16:42] Jenna Lee: And we want to start a pilot in January.

[16:45] Vivek Kulkarni: That aligns with our pilot LTS cut schedule.

[16:49] Dan Whitaker: I want to get very specific: if we file a ticket for backport, what happens?

[16:55] Noah Patel: Process: you open a support ticket referencing the issue and your LTS version. Support escalates to runtime backport owner. We triage eligibility tier. If eligible, we create a backport PR onto the LTS branch. That PR includes risk label, test plan, and links. Once it passes CI + perf suite, release eng schedules it for the next patch or an out-of-band.

[17:18] Dan Whitaker: And if it’s not eligible?

[17:20] Noah Patel: We give a rationale and alternatives: workaround, or upgrade to newer LTS line when available, or mainline if you can.

[17:30] Miguel Santos: For audit, is the support ticket linked in the PR?

[17:34] Connor O'Brien: Yes, we include references. Sometimes it’s a Jira SUP ID or internal. For your side, we can also reference your ticket ID in the notes.

[17:45] Priya Nair: We’d prefer not to leak internal ticket IDs publicly.

[17:48] Connor O'Brien: Totally. For customer-specific info, we can keep it in the customer comms. The public release notes will reference generic issue IDs or internal PRs, depending.

[18:01] Miguel Santos: That’s fine.

[18:04] Jenna Lee: Another question: do you support on-prem air gapped? Eventually.

[18:09] Vivek Kulkarni: Yes, but for this LTS topic, the artifacts need to be mirrorable. For air-gapped, we provide a bundle with checksums and signatures.

[18:20] Miguel Santos: Good.

[18:22] Dan Whitaker: I’m going to push on “monthly patches.” If there’s nothing, do you still ship something?

[18:29] Connor O'Brien: Not necessarily. We can do “no-op” month where there is no patch. But we’ll still publish status like “no changes this month.”

[18:38] Priya Nair: Actually we like that. Predictable communication.

[18:42] Connor O'Brien: On release notes format: we’re building sections: Summary, Who should upgrade, Risk level, Changes by category (security/correctness/perf), Known issues, Upgrade steps, Rollback steps.

[18:59] Jenna Lee: Include perf deltas.

[19:01] Connor O'Brien: Yep, perf deltas vs baseline.

[19:05] Dan Whitaker: p95 and p99.

[19:07] Connor O'Brien: Yep.

[19:10] (brief silence)

[19:12] Priya Nair: How does this compare to, say, AWS managed endpoints? They do patching under the hood. We do not want surprise patching.

[19:21] Connor O'Brien: We won’t auto-patch your Private deployment. Hosted we manage. For Private, you control upgrades, and LTS is about making those upgrades less risky.

[19:32] Jenna Lee: Together.ai claims “stable endpoints” but it’s still opaque.

[19:36] Connor O'Brien: Right. Our differentiation is explicit artifacts, explicit version pinning, and evidence.

[19:43] Miguel Santos: Evidence is big. Auditors don’t accept “trust us.”

[19:47] Naomi Feldman: Understood.

[19:50] Dan Whitaker: Can we talk about failure modes? Like, what happens if an LTS patch fails your perf threshold but fixes a security issue.

[19:58] Sahana Iyer: Great question. In that case, we’d likely proceed but mark it high risk and include mitigations. Or we’d attempt an alternative implementation. Security might override perf if it’s critical. But we would not silently ship; it would be an explicit callout.

[20:15] Priya Nair: And would we have time to test before it becomes “required”?

[20:19] Connor O'Brien: Yes. We can provide an RC (release candidate) artifact to enterprise customers under NDA/limited distribution, so you can validate before GA.

[20:30] Jenna Lee: RC would help.

[20:33] Miguel Santos: RC distribution must be controlled.

[20:36] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[20:39] Dan Whitaker: Another nuance: sometimes we need a fix backported but we can’t take other fixes bundled with it.

[20:46] Connor O'Brien: For LTS, we try to keep patches small, but it’s still a patch set. For truly urgent single-fix, we can do an out-of-band patch with minimal payload.

[20:59] Priya Nair: Okay.

[21:01] Connor O'Brien: Maybe we should talk about what you want contractually. Miguel, what does your audit ask for exactly? Like SOC2 report, plus release evidence?

[21:10] Miguel Santos: We need SOC2, yes. For release evidence, we need a process description and sample packet. Specifically: approvals, test results, artifact integrity verification, and change management logs.

[21:26] Naomi Feldman: We can provide process docs and sample evidence. For each LTS release, we can give you a standard evidence bundle.

[21:34] Miguel Santos: And retention? How long do you keep that evidence.

[21:39] Naomi Feldman: We are aligning on retention that meets enterprise needs. Likely at least the support window plus a buffer.

[21:48] Priya Nair: From ops side, I need the upgrade playbook to be explicit: commands, what to check, rollback steps.

[21:55] Vivek Kulkarni: We will provide a Private LTS upgrade/rollback guide. It’ll include version pinning in Helm, required preflight checks (disk space, GPU driver version), and post-upgrade validation: health endpoints, latency dashboards, error rates.

[22:11] Dan Whitaker: And like, “how to roll back and validate.”

[22:13] Vivek Kulkarni: Exactly.

[22:16] Jenna Lee: We also need to know what not to do, like “do not downgrade across X.”

[22:22] Vivek Kulkarni: Yes.

[22:24] Connor O'Brien: Let’s do a quick scenario. Suppose you are on 1.20-lts.2 and we publish 1.20-lts.3. What do you expect?

[22:32] Priya Nair: We expect minimal changes, risk clearly stated, and the ability to roll back to .2 without weirdness.

[22:40] Dan Whitaker: Plus clear regression gates. Like you’re not shipping a patch that regressed your own canary.

[22:46] Connor O'Brien: Right.

[22:47] Jenna Lee: And release notes that say “we changed scheduling fairness” is a red flag.

[22:53] Noah Patel: Which we won’t do.

[22:55] Miguel Santos: And we expect artifact signatures to validate, and hash to match, and tag immutable.

[23:03] Connor O'Brien: All aligned.

[23:05] (minor audio glitch)

[23:07] Sahana Iyer: One more build thing: for LTS, we’re also adding checks to avoid “mismatched artifacts,” like runtime binary and container mismatch. That’s a class of release race we’ve seen.

[23:20] Dan Whitaker: Good. That’s scary.

[23:22] Priya Nair: Another question: will LTS cover both dedicated and private? We do private now but might move to dedicated.

[23:30] Connor O'Brien: Same LTS line applies. That’s the goal: consistent runtime bits across deploy modes.

[23:37] Jenna Lee: Any differences per region?

[23:40] Connor O'Brien: For hosted/dedicated, region-specific is mostly infrastructure. Runtime artifact is the same.

[23:48] Priya Nair: Okay. I think we’ve hit the key points. Can you send us something concrete? A draft policy.

[23:55] Connor O'Brien: Yes. We’ll send: LTS channel overview, the backport policy, and a sample “pilot” release notes so you can see the format.

[24:06] Miguel Santos: And sample evidence packet.

[24:09] Naomi Feldman: We can provide a sample structure and what fields it contains. We’ll confirm what we can share.

[24:17] Dan Whitaker: I’d also like the canary plan. Like what you recommend.

[24:21] Vivek Kulkarni: We have an SRE-authored canary/rollout plan we can share at a high level.

[24:27] Dan Whitaker: Great.

[24:30] Jenna Lee: One last: if we need a backport, do we talk to Support or directly to you?

[24:36] Connor O'Brien: Start with Support so it’s tracked. For enterprise we’ll have an escalation path to the runtime backport owner.

[24:45] Priya Nair: Okay.

[24:47] Connor O'Brien: Any other questions before we wrap? We have time.

[24:51] Miguel Santos: Just confirming: your LTS commitment won’t block you from shipping new features on mainline, right?

[24:57] Connor O'Brien: Correct. LTS is separate. It’s meant to reduce churn for you while preserving velocity elsewhere.

[25:05] Priya Nair: That’s what we want.

[25:08] Connor O'Brien: Cool. Let’s do next steps. I’ll email docs tomorrow. Noah will summarize the tiers/approval. Sahana will list CI gates and what evidence you get. Naomi will set up a security/GRC session for provenance. Vivek will send Private pinning/rollback guide.

[25:27] Priya Nair: Works for us.

[25:28] Dan Whitaker: Thanks all.

[25:30] Miguel Santos: Thank you.

[25:31] Jenna Lee: Thanks.

[25:33] Connor O'Brien: Alright, talk soon.

(Transcript ends; remainder of recording contained no additional discussion.)
